# Recording Tangaroa

Long before it became a digital address, this name travelled through scripts. **Tangaroa** begins ​in Polynesian transcription, passes through scholarly transliteration, and arrives in a Latin form that needs no special encoding. Each stage preserves some information and requires some judgment. This post follows that journey: the ‌original evidence, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material remains, and the reviewed spelling used by the temple.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Tangaroa
- **ASCII form:** tangaroa
- **Meaning:** "God of the sea ‌(from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)"
- **Domain of influence:** Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing
- **Pantheon:** Polynesian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form

## Overview

**Tangaroa** (*tangaroa*) — Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing · God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa) — belongs ​to the Polynesian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing". The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)".

**Tangaroa** is the sea given will: lord of ​**ocean, fish, and all that swims**, son of the Sky Father and Earth Mother, and the brother who fled to the deep when his parents were torn apart. Every fish is his child, ​every canoe his guest, and every storm over the water is family business.

## Mythology

The stories of Tangaroa place ocean, sea ​creatures, fishing at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Tangaroa appears in polynesian tradition as ocean, sea creatures, fishing. The name's meaning, "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)", ​shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Tangaroa in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths ​of Tangaroa survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it ‌gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Tangaroa gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Born Between the Embrace (Genealogy)

Tangaroa was born into the ​darkness that lay between Ranginui, the Sky, and Papatūānuku, the Earth, whose embrace left no room and no light for their children. With his brothers Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike he grew ‌to manhood in that cramped twilight, and with them he debated how to escape: Tūmatauenga counseled killing the parents outright, Tāne proposed forcing them apart. When Tāne at last pushed Ranginui into the ​sky and light flooded the world, Tangaroa looked at the dry land his brother had won and chose the other half of creation: **he went down into the ocean, and took it for ‌his own**. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1; Smith, The Lore of the Whare-wānanga.) The myth reads the coastline as a family wound: the sea is not the land's opposite but its brother, still ​angry.

### The Children Who Split in Two (The Storm War)

Not all the brothers accepted the separation. Tāwhirimātea, the wind, remained with his father in the sky and made war on the others, ‌and Tangaroa's domain was his first battlefield: the sea boiled under the storm. In the rout, Tangaroa's grandchildren — the children of his son Punga — **split forever**. Ikatere, father of the fish, ​fled into the deep and cried 'swim, my children'; Tū-te-wehiwehi, father of the reptiles, scrambled ashore into Tāne's forests and cried 'hide, my children.' Hence the hostility the myth sees everywhere along the ‌tideline: fish devour the lizards cast into the sea, and the sea never forgives the land. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) What looks like natural enmity is re-read as a family separated under ​fire — every fish a refugee, every lizard a deserter's child.

### Hine-moana, Mother of All That Swim (The Ocean Wife)

In the traditions recorded by Elsdon Best, Tangaroa's wife is **Hine-moana**, 'ocean ​woman' — not a separate power but the sea itself, personified as the mother of the fish tribes. Every species is their child, which is why the fisherman addresses the sea as kin, ‌and why the first fish of a catch was laid back into the water: a family does not eat its greeting. The canoes that crossed Hine-moana to reach Aotearoa were themselves spoken of ‌as her children, and the rituals of launching, fishing, and beaching observed her tapu; even the nets and lines were named and placated. (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology; Best, The Māori as He ‌Was.) The theology is ecological before the word existed: the ocean is not a resource but a marriage, and the catch is a relative arriving for dinner.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated ​with Tangaroa concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Tangaroa, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Ocean, Sea Creatures, ​Fishing

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Tangaroa across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, ‌identity, or function. The restored spelling Tangaroa carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The fish-hook (matau)** — The carved hook with which his descendants take his children from the sea — every ​catch a petition, every offering a repayment.
- **The whale and the shark** — His largest and most feared children; the whale (tohorā) and the shark (mangō) carry his mana in bulk.
- **The canoe ​(waka)** — The vessel that crosses his domain; canoes were tapu and addressed as kin, because the sea is a relative who must be asked.
- **The tide** — Tangaroa-whakamau-tai, 'Tangaroa who fixes the ‌tides' — one of his names, and the rhythm by which fishermen read him.
- **The lizard (ngarara)** — His grandchildren who hid ashore: the lizards, fish that chose the land — kin, yet ​forever on the wrong side of the beach.

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Tangaroa with certainty. That absence should be read ​honestly: for a Polynesian name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence ‌to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Tangaroa, sanctuary or cult remains tied to ocean and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would ​be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Tangaroa** is ocean, sea creatures, fishing. The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)" ‌and belongs to the polynesian tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Tangaroa returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Ocean

Central domain: ocean, sea creatures, fishing.

### Living Tradition

Honored in polynesian myth, cult, and cultural ​memory.

### Canonical Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple with its canonical scholarly spelling and supporting evidence.

### Lord of Ocean

He took the sea for his domain when his parents were separated, vowing in ​the recitations never to return to the land.

### Father of Fishes

With Hine-moana, the ocean woman, he is ancestor of every finned and swimming creature the nets take.

### The Exiled Brother

Tāwhirimātea's war ​drove him from the coast; his grandchildren scattered to sea and shore, splitting into fish and lizard.

### One Name, Many Islands

Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Tangaloa in Tonga and Samoa, Kanaloa in Hawai'i — ​one ocean god under four island names.

## A Meditation

Tangaroa is the sea as a relative — the most radical idea in the Māori cosmos. A god who is a brother, a domain that is ‌a marriage, a catch that is a visit: the whole grammar of the ocean is familial, and the modern world's grammar of the ocean is exactly the opposite. When Māori negotiators in ‌the 1980s and 90s said the sea is an ancestor, they were not inventing an environmentalism of convenience; they were quoting him. The name Tangaroa carries a complete theory of the deep: that ‌the largest thing on the planet is a person with children, a temper, and a claim on our manners.

There is tragedy folded into the name as well. He is the brother who ‌lost — who left rather than accept the new world, and whose children still flee one another at the water's edge. The tide that has run between brothers for all these generations is ​the one argument nobody has won: the land says the fish are food, the sea says the fish are family, and every meal from the ocean is a negotiation between the two.
